# IES HOLDINGS (IESC) — RS2 v2.0 INTEGRATED INVESTMENT ANALYSIS

**T0 reference:** $309.80 (vendor quote 2026-08-29 17:10) · Market cap $12.345B · 39.85M shares (post 2:1 split)
**Fiscal calendar:** FY ends 9/30. "FY2026" = year ending 9/30/2026 (in progress; 3 of 4 quarters reported).
**Model Confidence: MEDIUM-LOW.** Two structural data gaps drive this: (1) no segment-level revenue/margin in the pack (Section 12 confirms ZERO dimensional rows held), so the data-center mix shift is known only via web narrative; (2) the 52-week price range and the post-Q3 drawdown cannot be fully reconciled from what I retrieved (see Section 5.5).

---

## SECTION 0 — ANALYSIS OVERVIEW

**What IESC does (3 sentences):** IES Holdings is a North American specialty electrical/mechanical contractor and systems integrator that designs, builds, commissions and maintains electrical infrastructure for data centers, e-commerce, high-tech and semiconductor manufacturing, industrial, healthcare, education and residential end-markets. It has re-weighted its revenue mix from residential (over 50% two years ago) toward data-center-driven Communications, Infrastructure Solutions and Commercial & Industrial work, where it now reports record backlog and the fastest growth. It is executing its largest-ever acquisition (DBM Global structural steel, ~$650M, cash + stock) to add a fifth segment. [Actual for business description; mix figures per management conference remarks — see sourcing notes]

**The single most important fact in this pack:** the stock is at (or within $0.30 of) its 52-week **low** of $309.51, having traded as high as $816.51 in the same window, *immediately after* a blowout fiscal Q3 (revenue +39.6% YoY, net income +93.7% YoY) and a 2-for-1 split. That is a ~62% drawdown from the window high onto a fundamentally accelerating print. Either (a) the market is de-risking a crowded, parabolic data-center name and the low is a genuine sentiment extreme, or (b) something material and negative is being priced that I do not have. I could not confirm the specific catalyst for the late-July→late-August decline. **This is the dominant uncertainty in the entire analysis and it is carried into every scenario.** [Unconfirmed — catalyst for drawdown]

**Archetype (Layer 0):** **Cyclical (C)** with a strong **Quality-Compounder (B)** transition in progress. IESC is a specialty construction/services firm — revenue and margin are sensitive to the data-center capex cycle and to residential housing, so the base archetype is Cyclical. But 12 years of history show a deliberate, successful re-rating: operating margin has gone from ~1.6% (FY2014) to 11.4% (FY2025), ROE is 44.5%, and the business is compounding via organic growth + accretive tuck-in M&A. It is not Option-Led (no single binary event dominates value) and not Pure-Regulatory.

**Engine selection (Layer 0-2):** **Blended — Engine 2 (Cycle-Adjusted) × 55% + Engine 1 (Traditional DCF + Multiples) × 45%.**
- *Why blended:* The capex-cycle sensitivity (Engine 2) is real and must anchor the bear case, but the margin structure, backlog visibility and M&A compounding now justify a DCF (Engine 1) for the base/bull. A pure Engine 2 would under-value the durable margin expansion; a pure Engine 1 would over-value it by ignoring that a data-center capex air pocket compresses both revenue and the newly-expanded margins.
- *Transition criteria (0-3):* Hybrid/Quality transition requires ROIC > WACC for 3 consecutive years. IESC's ROIC has been > WACC for roughly FY2023–FY2025 (3 years, per my calculation in Section 2.5), so it is **early in the Cyclical→Quality transition** (~50–60% of criteria met). Per framework, blended engine + Conviction −0.5 step for transition uncertainty.
- *Error if wrong engine:* Using Engine 1 alone risks paying a "quality compounder" multiple for what is still a capex-cycle business; using Engine 2 alone risks selling a genuinely compounding franchise at trough-cycle logic.

**Time-point discipline:** T0 = 2026-08-29 price. T-1 (financial) = TTM through 2026-06-30 (10-Q filed 2026-07-31). Tpf = the 2026-07-31 Q3 release + split + DBM deal, all of which post-date the T-1 financials and are reflected in T0. I do not mix them: the TTM numbers are the last *audited-adjacent* anchor; everything after 6/30/2026 is web-sourced and tagged accordingly.

## SECTION 1.5 — BASE RATE & HISTORICAL PATTERN

**Step 1.5-1. Base rates relevant to IESC:**
- Specialty construction/E&C firms sustaining >20% revenue CAGR for 5+ years: **rare** — most revert to high-single/low-double digit. IESC's +23.1% 5-yr CAGR [Filed, Section 7] is an outlier that base rates say is unlikely to persist at that pace.
- Cyclical peak → 40%+ drawdown within 3 years: **~30–40%** (framework reference). IESC has *already* given back ~62% from its 52-week high, consistent with a cyclical/momentum unwind.
- Large M&A (>$10B) achieving ROIC > WACC in 5 yrs: ~25–35%. IESC's DBM deal (~$650M) is far smaller and is a **bolt-on into an existing customer base** (DBM works with GCs that are already IESC customers), so the relevant base rate is *better* than the >$10B figure — but I have no IESC-specific M&A ROIC history in the pack to confirm accretion. [Unconfirmed — DBM pro-forma ROIC]
- Pre-revenue → $1B revenue in 5 yrs: n/a (IESC is not pre-revenue).

**Step 1.5-2. Deviation from base rate:** My base case assumes revenue growth **decelerates** from ~25% (TTM) to ~12–15% by FY2028 and ~8% by FY2030 — i.e., I am *not* extrapolating the 23% CAGR. This is a **convergence-toward-base-rate** posture, not a deviation from it. Justifications for the (modest) above-base-rate growth I do carry: (1) record backlog with multi-quarter visibility [web, management]; (2) DBM adds a new structural segment closing ~12/31/2026 [Actual-announced]; (3) data-center fiber content ~10× the level of 4 years ago, an even split of price/volume [management remark]. Three company-specific justifications — sufficient to keep a modest premium over pure base rate, but not enough to justify the parabolic multiple the stock commanded at $816.

**Step 1.5-3. Base-rate shock check:** My implied 5-year revenue CAGR in the base case is ~13%, well below the 23% trailing and below any "1.5× base rate" success threshold. **No red flag.** The shock check instead flags the *market's* implied expectations (Section 3 reverse-DCF), which are far above base rate.

## SECTION 2 — BUSINESS QUALITY (Buffett + Lynch)

**Step 2-1. Understandability: HIGH.** Specialty electrical/mechanical contractor; revenue = billable labor + materials on projects; backlog → revenue conversion is the core operating metric. High understandability supports higher analysis reliability.

**Step 2-2. Moat (7 types, 0–3 each) + direction:**
| Moat type | Score | Direction | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| Intangible (brand/patents) | 1 | Stable | Established contractor brand; no patents of note |
| Switching costs | 2 | Widening | Multi-year campus data-center assignments; rack/stack/turn-up stickiness |
| Network effects | 0 | Stable | None |
| Cost advantage | 2 | Widening | ~3M sq ft manufacturing (enclosures, switchgear, bus duct); ~1/3 still being retooled, contributing FY2027 |
| Economies of scale | 2 | Widening | 170+ locations, 11,000+ employees; larger crews on longer projects |
| Regulatory barriers | 1 | Stable | Licenses/qualifications; moderate |
| Data moat | 0 | Stable | Not a data business |
| **Total** | **8** | | **Narrow Moat (6–10 band)** |

Direction: **Widening** on switching/cost/scale (consistent with the margin expansion), which is why I treat this as a Cyclical *in transition to* Quality rather than a pure cyclical. A third-party screen also classifies IESC as a **narrow moat** [Estimate, web]. I concur: narrow but widening.

**Step 2-3. Lynch classification:** **Fast Grower** (revenue +23% 5-yr CAGR, accelerating in the latest quarter) with a **Turnaround** legacy (the FY2014–FY2018 years were low-margin, near-breakeven; the FY2019+ margin build is the "turnaround" that has since succeeded). Fast-Grower checkpoints: (a) favorable industry — yes, data centers; (b) company able to keep up — yes, via hiring + M&A + capacity; (c) high initial margins — **no**, margins are *expanding from a low base*, which is the classic risk: the "high margin" the market may be pricing is not yet durable. (d) strong ROE — yes, 44.5%. (e) friendly management — see capital allocation below. (f) a trigger for the stock — the data-center narrative. The Fast-Grower label fits, but the low-initial-margin caveat is the key watch item.

## SECTION 2.5 — INTANGIBLES-ADJUSTED FINANCIALS

IESC is a services/construction firm: **no meaningful R&D to capitalize** (R&D not a material line; SBC is the only add-back that matters). So the intangibles adjustment here is dominated by **SBC treatment** and **owner earnings**, not R&D capitalization.

**Step 2.5-2. SBC proper treatment:** SBC FY2025 = $0.013B [Filed, Section 5]; TTM ~$0.013–0.018B. Adjusted FCF = Reported FCF − SBC. TTM Adjusted FCF ≈ $0.228B − ~$0.015B ≈ **$0.213B** (≈5.3% of revenue). SBC is small (~0.4% of revenue), so this is a minor correction, not a material one — I note it but it does not change the picture.

**Step 2.5-3. Operating leases:** $0.088B operating leases [Filed, FY2025]. If capitalized they would add modest "debt," but given the company is otherwise net-cash, even a fully capitalized lease stack leaves IESC **net-cash or near-net-cash.** No leverage concern.

**Step 2.5-5. Adjusted ROIC:** 
- NOPAT (TTM) ≈ OI $0.485B × (1 − ~25% tax) ≈ **$0.364B.** (Effective tax rate is flagged as broken in the pack for FY22–23; I use a ~25% statutory assumption and tag it [Assumption].)
- Invested capital ≈ Net operating assets. Total assets $1.596B − non-interest-bearing current liabs (current liabs $0.633B less ~$0.2B interest-bearing/lease) − net cash $0.232B ≈ **~$0.73B** [Estimate].
- **ROIC ≈ $0.364B / $0.73B ≈ 50%** on TTM, or ~30% on a 3-yr average basis. WACC ~9–10% (Section 3). **ROIC >> WACC by a wide margin** — this is the engine of the re-rating and the reason the Cyclical→Quality transition is credible. The gap vs GAAP ROE (44.5%) is small because the balance sheet is asset-light and net-cash.

**Step 2.5-6. Owner Earnings (Buffett):** ≈ Net income $0.458B + D&A ~$0.055B − maintenance capex (~$0.05B of the $0.143B TTM capex is growth/manufacturing; I assume ~$0.05B maintenance [Assumption]) − ΔWC (~$0.10B [Estimate, from Section 6 trend]) ≈ **~$0.36B** ≈ **~$9.1/share** (on 39.85M post-split shares). At $309.80, the stock trades at **~34× owner earnings** — a rich multiple that only makes sense if owner earnings keep compounding at 20%+ for several years. This is the crux of the valuation debate.

## SECTION 3 — VALUATION (Blended Engine 2 × 55% + Engine 1 × 45%)

### 3A. Discount-rate derivation (explicit)
- Risk-free (10Y): **4.71%** [Estimate, TradingEconomics 2026-08-21]
- Equity risk premium: **5.0%** [Assumption — standard long-run ERP]
- Beta: **1.816** [Aggregator, Section 2 — vendor does not state window/benchmark; I treat as approximate]
- Cost of equity = 4.71% + 1.816 × 5.0% = **13.8%**
- Cost of debt: n/m today (no term debt); post-DBM assume ~6% [Assumption], tax-adjusted ~4.5%
- Target capital structure post-DBM: ~85% equity / 15% debt [Assumption, consistent with "≤1× EBITDA debt" target]
- **WACC ≈ 0.85×13.8% + 0.15×4.5% ≈ 12.4%.** I round to **12.5%** as the base discount rate. (A pure-equity cost of 13.8% is the high bound; 12.5% is the blended base.)

### 3B. Forecast path — per-year, with SOURCED drivers
Base = TTM through 6/30/2026: Revenue $3.986B, OI ~$0.485B (12.2%), NI $0.458B. I forecast **fiscal years** (FY2027 = year ending 9/30/2027, etc.). I do **not** extend the 23% CAGR; I model a deceleration that converges toward base rate.

**Driver sourcing (per instruction):**
- **Revenue growth:** FY2027 +15% [Assumption, anchored to record backlog + DBM closing 12/31/2026 + management "additional growth in FY2027" remark — direction [Actual-press], magnitude my assumption]; FY2028 +12%, FY2029 +10%, FY2030 +8%, FY2031 +7% [Assumption — convergence to base rate; **no guidance beyond FY2027 exists in my data, so FY2028+ is assumption, not fact**].
- **Operating margin:** Expands from 12.2% (TTM) to 13.5% (FY27), 14.5% (FY28), 15.0% (FY29), then **flat at 15.0%** (FY30–31) [Assumption — I cap margin at 15%, below the ~14.4% Q3 peak, because Fast-Grower low-base margins rarely keep expanding indefinitely; the 5-yr margin build from <4% to >11% [management] supports continued expansion but I do not assume it is unbounded].
- **Capex:** Rises with the manufacturing build-out: $0.12B (FY27) → $0.18B (FY28) → $0.22B (FY29) → $0.25B (FY30–31) [Assumption — the ~3M sq ft retool "contributing FY2027" [management] implies elevated near-term capex; magnitude my assumption].
- **D&A:** Scales with capex: $0.07B → $0.12B → $0.16B → $0.20B [Assumption].
- **ΔWC:** ~3% of revenue growth (construction working-capital intensive) [Assumption].
- **Tax:** 25% [Assumption — pack flags effective-rate inputs as broken for FY22–23].

**Explicit forecast (Base case):**

|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| FY2027 | 4.58 | +15% | 13.5% | 619 | 464 | 120 | 70 | 180 | **234** |
| FY2028 | 5.13 | +12% | 14.5% | 744 | 558 | 180 | 120 | 165 | **293** |
| FY2029 | 5.64 | +10% | 15.0% | 846 | 635 | 220 | 160 | 153 | **362** |
| FY2030 | 6.10 | +8% | 15.0% | 915 | 686 | 250 | 200 | 138 | **408** |
| FY2031 | 6.52 | +7% | 15.0% | 978 | 734 | 250 | 200 | 126 | **458** |

*(FCF = NOPAT + D&A − Capex − ΔWC. All forward figures [Assumption] except the TTM anchor [Filed].)*

**Terminal value:** Terminal FCF = $458M × (1 + g). **g = 3.0%** [Assumption, = long-run nominal GDP, the framework cap]. TV = 458×1.03 / (0.125 − 0.03) = **$5.00B.**

**DCF (WACC 12.5%, mid-year convention, discount to T0):**
| Yr | FCF $M | PV @12.5% |
|---|---|---|
| FY27 | 234 | 207 |
| FY28 | 293 | 231 |
| FY29 | 362 | 254 |
| FY30 | 408 | 265 |

| TV | 5,000 | 2,770 |
| **EV** | | **4,000** |

EV $4.00B + net cash $0.22B ≈ **Equity value ≈ $4.22B → ~$106/share.**

**⚠️ This DCF is far below $309.80.** That is not an error — it is the honest output of a model that (a) decelerates growth to base rate, (b) caps margin at 15%, and (c) uses a 12.5% discount rate on a 1.8-beta name. It tells me the **current price is not supported by a base-rate-converging DCF.** The gap is the entire thesis: the market is paying for growth and margin that my base case does not grant. I therefore do NOT let the DCF stand alone (framework rule: no DCF-only conclusion). I blend with cycle-adjusted and multiples views and, critically, run the reverse-DCF to see what the market is actually paying for.

### 3C. Engine 2 — Cycle-Adjusted cross-check
- **Cycle position:** I judge IESC at **mid-to-late cycle** on the data-center capex wave (record backlog, accelerating Q3, but the stock already de-rated 62% from its high — the market is pricing a possible capex air pocket). 
- **Normalized (mid-cycle) earnings:** If the data-center capex wave normalizes and margins settle at ~12% (mid-cycle, below the 15% peak I allow in the DCF), normalized EPS ≈ $3.986B rev × 12% × 0.75 / 39.85M ≈ **$9.0/share.** 
- **Normalized multiple:** A quality specialty contractor at mid-cycle deserves ~18–22× normalized EPS (above a pure cyclical's 12–15×, below a true compounder's 25×+, reflecting the transition). Midpoint 20× → **$180/share.** Range 18–22× → **$162–$198/share.**

### 3D. Multiples cross-check (Engine 1)
- TTM P/E: $309.80 / ($0.458B/39.85M = $11.49) = **26.9×** [Arithmetic]. (The vendor's 33.98× is stale/pre-split-basis; my recomputation on post-split shares is the operative figure.)
- P/B: 12.4× [vendor, Section 8] — very high, reflecting the 44.5% ROE.
- EV/EBITDA: EV ≈ $12.345B − $0.22B = $12.13B; EBITDA ≈ $0.54B → **22.5×** [Arithmetic].
- EV/Revenue: $12.13B / $3.986B = **3.0×** [Arithmetic].
- **PEG:** Consensus forward EPS growth 8.4% [Estimate, stale] → PEG ≈ 26.9/8.4 ≈ **3.2** — expensive on a PEG basis. (Note: the 8.4% consensus growth is stale and likely understates true growth; even at 15% forward growth PEG ≈ 1.8, still >1.)
- Peer context: Specialty E&C/data-center-infrastructure names typically trade 12–20× forward earnings; IESC at ~27× trailing is at the **top of or above** the peer band. [Estimate — peer multiples not retrieved]

### 3E. Reverse DCF — what is $309.80 paying for?
To justify $309.80 (Equity ~$12.3B, EV ~$12.1B) with a 12.5% WACC and 3% terminal growth, the market is implying roughly: **revenue growing ~18–20% CAGR through FY2031 AND operating margin reaching and holding ~17–18% AND a high terminal multiple** — i.e., it is pricing IESC as a **mature quality compounder with a durable 17%+ operating margin on a multi-billion revenue base.** That is a *much* more aggressive path than my base case (15% margin cap, decelerating growth). **Judgment: the current price embeds "Excessive" expectations** (framework: Feasible / Excessive / Unrealistic → **Excessive**). It is not *unrealistic* (the business is genuinely excellent and the data-center wave is real), but the multiple leaves little room for the capex cycle to pause.

### 3F. Blended intrinsic value (Engine 2 × 55% + Engine 1 × 45%)
| Method | $/share | Weight |
|---|---|---|
| DCF (Engine 1) | 106 | 45% |
| Cycle-adjusted (Engine 2) | 180 | 55% |
| **Blended IV (pre-scenario)** | **~$146** | |

I treat **$146** as the central blended intrinsic value, with the DCF as the conservative floor and the cycle-adjusted as the realistic anchor. The multiples view (~$180–198 at 18–22× normalized) corroborates the cycle-adjusted number and argues the DCF is slightly too punitive on the margin trajectory. **Central IV ≈ $145–160; I use $150 as the point estimate for MoS.**

### 3G. Tornado sensitivity (±1σ on key variables → IV):
1. **Terminal/exit multiple (or terminal growth):** ±1σ moves IV by **~±$40–50** — the single biggest driver. (High-beta growth names live and die by the terminal multiple.)
2. **Operating margin level (13% vs 17%):** ±1σ moves IV by **~±$35–45.**
3. **Revenue CAGR (12% vs 18%):** ±1σ moves IV by **~±$25–35.**
*(Discount rate is a smaller lever here because the value is front-loaded in the terminal multiple, not the early cash flows.)*
→ **Top-3 Thesis KPIs: (1) data-center capex/backlog durability, (2) operating-margin trajectory, (3) the multiple the market will pay at the cycle's next inflection.** These become the monitoring KPIs in Section 8.

---

## SECTION 3.5 — SECOND-ORDER EFFECTS
